frameworks.name: Cart Close Sequencing for Membership Launch
frameworks.definition: A two-phase launch strategy that maximizes annual prepayment by closing the annual tier with exclusive bonuses first, then reopening with monthly-only option at lower value.

frameworks.name: Physical Product Premium Bundle
frameworks.definition: Bundling a tangible product (e.g., printer, paper kit) with a digital membership to increase conversion willingness and justify higher price points to end users.

claims.text: Membership businesses collecting $60 in cash within 30 days while spending $90 on customer acquisition cannot scale profitably on an evergreen basis without restructuring their cash collection.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Low initial cash collection relative to CAC
claims.mechanism: The founder must collect payment in advance of work delivery and take acquisition costs upfront, requiring 6+ months to break even rather than the 1-2 month target.

numbers.axis: Cash collection and acquisition cost ratio

bounded_by: Assumes membership churn of 93% and LTV of $300 (or $385 calculated)

claims.text: In a five-day event selling to a consumer audience, the impulse purchase window is $300-$600; pricing below this range (e.g., recurring $27/month) leaves money on the table and prevents sufficient upfront cash collection.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Consumers at events have heightened purchase intent and capital availability in short windows; pricing in the $300-$600 range aligns with psychological willingness to spend on discretionary offerings.

numbers.axis: Impulse purchase price window for consumer event sales

bounded_by: Does not apply to B2B sales or long-consideration-cycle purchases

claims.text: Offering annual membership with exclusive bonuses (not offered to monthly subscribers) during an event, then removing those bonuses post-event to run a 'scoop-up campaign' to the $27/month offer, creates a psychological anchor that makes monthly pricing feel like a discount while extending the effective prepayment window.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Sequential cart closes (annual first, then monthly)
claims.mechanism: Exclusive bonuses tied to annual commitment anchor premium pricing during the event; post-event removal signals bonus cost to monthly buyers, making the $27 option feel like a forced downgrade rather than an alternative, reducing takes while preserving repeat customer potential.
bounded_by: Requires clear bonus communication and transparency (do not misrepresent monthly offering as including bonuses)

claims.text: Adding a physical product (printer, paper kit, or bundled materials) to a digital membership offer increases consumer willingness to purchase and can justify doubling or tripling the price point because the physical product provides tangible legitimacy for the purchase.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Product has a physical component that end user can justify to a third party (spouse, family)
Item cost is manageable for bundling (e.g., printer <$300)
claims.mechanism: Physical products provide psychological justification (an 'excuse') for purchase that digital-only offers lack. A consumer can rationalize the spend to a spouse by pointing to the tangible asset: 'I got this printer so I can generate income,' not just a digital login.

numbers.axis: Price lift from physical product bundling

bounded_by: Only applicable when product delivery is feasible (not fully digital-only services)

claims.text: LTV of a membership at 7% monthly churn (93% retention) is calculated by dividing annual price by the churn rate: a $270/year membership with 7% churn yields ~$385 LTV, which is a healthy 4.3x multiple over a typical $90 CAC.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: LTV calculation from membership pricing and churn

bounded_by: Assumes stable churn over time; does not account for seasonal variations or launch-specific cohort effects

claims.text: To confirm LTV and troubleshoot churn, a membership business should implement cohort tracking (e.g., via Teachable or manual tracking) to follow a single cohort of customers from the launch month through their lifetime; this reveals whether churn is uniform or concentrated in early months.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Cohort-level tracking is available or can be manually implemented
claims.mechanism: Cohort tracking allows differentiation between stable long-term retention and early-stage front-loaded churn; without it, blended churn figures hide the true shape of customer lifetime value.
bounded_by: Most manual tracking requires light data engineering; some platforms (Teachable, others) do this automatically

examples.text: A sticker-crafting membership business generating $1.2M revenue with $27/month or $270/year annual pricing across a primarily 45+ female audience runs paid ads generating $90 CAC while collecting only $60 in cash within the first 30 days. The founder reports true LTV (across all members) is ~$300-$385, but spends six months recovering ad costs rather than the desired one month. By shifting to annual-only during events with exclusive bonuses and then mopping up with a lower-bonus monthly offer afterward, the founder can compress breakeven to two months or faster.

During a five-day paid event ($10 entry) selling membership, the founder had been offering both $27/month and $270/year with the same incentive (no bonus differentiation). By reserving joining bonuses for annual-only membership during the event and later removing them for monthly offers in the post-event scoop-up campaign, the founder can signal value difference and make monthly pricing feel like a downgrade rather than an alternative.

A creative/crafts business could bundle the membership with a physical printer, ink, and sticker paper—items the customer will use to execute on the course content. This tangible asset justifies the purchase to a spouse ("I bought this so I can make money") and allows price testing at $500-$1000 instead of the $300-$600 digital-only ceiling.

practices.text: When running a five-day selling event for a membership, make the annual tier the exclusive offer during the event window, with clear annual-only bonuses. After the event closes, run a second cart-close phase with the monthly option ($27/month) but strip out 2-3 of the bonuses, keeping only 1 bonus to signal value difference.

If a prospect asks for monthly pricing during the event (or post-event), respond transparently: 'We offer monthly options, but you won't get these bonuses that I just spent time explaining, and they're valuable.' Do not lie, but you can make monthly less convenient relative to annual.

Track membership cohorts by launch month to separate stable long-term churn from early-stage cancellations; if your platform does not do this automatically (like Teachable), build a simple manual tracker or spreadsheet to follow one month's cohort.

Test adding a physical product to the membership offer in your next launch; even a single item (e.g., printer, sticker paper bundle) can justify a 2-3x price increase if it provides the end user with a tangible excuse to justify the purchase to a third party.
